rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology section - case study with semi-structured interviews (19 farmers, WUA presidents/secretaries, officials, technicians), policy document analysis and field observations in four municipalities of the C<U+00E0>nyoles watershed. Q2: Transformations 2-3 and Discussion - the shift to drip was accompanied by conversion of 1371 ha of former rain-fed slopes to drip (38.9% of irrigated area), a shift to citrus/kaki monocultures with higher crop water requirements, and the authors conclude that drip plus expansion and intensification led to more water use at watershed level, with wells drying and groundwater tables falling in the upper watershed. Q4: Transformation 2 (Figure 2, area statistics 1983-2014) and Transformation 3 (Table 1, crop areas; IVIA crop water requirements) quantify the intermediate variables - irrigated area expansion and shift to higher water-demanding crops - through which drip raised watershed water use. Q6: Discussion - results reported at watershed level across four municipalities (1739 ha converted, 1371 ha expanded). Q7: Transformations 1-2 - expansion occurred where well concessions and groundwater were available (Montesa, Vallada); in La Font de la Figuera lack of access to water hampered expansion and wells dried up in 2005, so groundwater access/concessions are stated as the enabling condition. Q8: Transformations section and Conclusions - authors state the transformations cannot be solely attributed to drip, as they also relate to broader changes in Spanish agriculture and society.
rows.notes: Increase in consumptive water use at watershed level is inferred from area and crop statistics and stakeholder reports (lowered water tables, dry wells), not measured directly. Expansion is supported by official statistics and interviews, but the water-use increase itself is not established by two independent methods, so Q3 conservatively no. Single watershed, one climate, so Q5 no. No dispersion measures reported.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology section - own case study with interviews, document analysis and field observations. Q2: Transformation 5 - authors report that in the study area canals used before the shift to drip have been abandoned or disused, only one ancient weir (Montesa) remains operational, and mills, pools and underground canals are abandoned; supported by interview quotes from WUA secretaries/presidents and farmers in Vallada and Moixent. Q6: Transformation 5 - heritage loss reported across the four villages of the watershed, not a single plot. Q7: Transformation 5 - authors state from their findings that the loss results from lack of maintenance because public administration does not prioritise water heritage and farmers cannot cope with maintenance costs. Q8: Transformations section and Conclusions - authors caution that the transformations cannot be solely attributed to drip irrigation.
rows.notes: Finding rests mainly on stakeholder interviews with some author statements; field observations are mentioned in methods but not explicitly tied to the heritage section, and part of the infrastructure description is drawn from Pelejero (2013), so Q3 conservatively no. No intermediate variable measured (Q4 no). Single watershed (Q5 no). No quantitative dispersion (Q9 no).

notes: Full text appears complete. Qualitative case study (interviews, official area statistics, field observation) in one Spanish watershed; no quantitative measurements of water consumption or statistical uncertainty.
